title: Your study
tomorrow: give without your name, or sign it so others give too?

cards: People say "my song" about a track they've played so often it feels like theirs. Psalm 1 does something like that, and at first it looks like a slip. The verse starts with "the law of the LORD."
A few words later, in the Hebrew, it's torato: his Torah. Whose? God's, or the reader's?

teach.b: Here's the line in the JPS translation: "But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in His law doth he meditate day and night." The translators capitalized that second His, reading it as God's. That's a fair reading.

teach.h: THEN, IN THE HEBREW: HIS TORAH.
teach.b: The Talmud hears something else in the Hebrew. At first, it says, the Torah is called the LORD's.

teach.h: LABOR OVER IT, AND IT'S YOURS.
teach.b: After a person has labored over it, it's called his own. So the puzzle is the point: the text starts out belonging to God, and with enough study, it also belongs to you.
Pirkei Avot has a sage with an unusual name, Ben Bag Bag, who says: turn it, and turn it, for everything is in it.
That's how a text becomes yours. Not by reading it once, but by coming back. A psalm.
A chapter of Avot. This week's portion. A page of Talmud with a study partner on the phone.
Something to tell a friend tonight: the Talmud reads Psalm 1 as saying the Torah becomes the student's own.

how: Jewish learners often keep a regular text, alone or with a chavruta (study partner): the weekly Torah portion, a chapter of Pirkei Avot, Psalms, or a daily page of Talmud.

o: a holy book you own but never open
the textbook assigned for your class
the text you've studied until it's yours

games.q: a text becomes yours — tap the pairs.
p: after study, it's called his own

s: the Talmud reads Psalm 1 as saying the Torah becomes the student's own
first it's called the LORD's; after study, it's called his.
the JPS 1917 English reads the second 'His' as the student's
it capitalizes 'His', reading it as God's; the Talmud hears the student in the Hebrew.
'turn it, and turn it' is a saying in Pirkei Avot
Ben Bag Bag says it, for everything is in it.

games.q: your teenage cousin says, 'i've read that psalm a hundred times. there's nothing left in it.' what fits Ben Bag Bag?
o: turn it again; everything is in it, and you've changed since last time.
move on; once you've read a text through, it's done.
only trained scholars ever find new things in old texts.
games.why: Ben Bag Bag: turn it, and turn it, for everything is in it. coming back is how a text becomes yours.

practice: Open your text, on paper or a screen, to a line you already know. Read it slowly three times. On the third time, look for one word you'd never noticed before, and stay with that word.

wordCard.voice: Your study: the text you keep coming back to, turned so often it becomes yours, as the Talmud reads Psalm 1.

carryVoice: Your line: your text, turned so often that it has turned you a little. Shalom, friend.
